    #216042. What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3130 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that last term in Little v.
    • On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.
    • Industry observers note that now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that last term in Little v. Hecox, which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ... You don't think that Brown and any of the other named plaintiffs that we have in famous cases dr[ew] … attention to those people as people?” Sotomayor asked the question in the context of Hecox requesting that the Supreme Court dismiss the case, citing, in part, “negative public scrutiny ... because of this litigation.”.

    On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

    Industry observers note that now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Each asked the Supreme Court to answer one of the most fundamental questions of all: Where does government power end and personal liberty begin?

    Joseph Lochner: Lochner v. New York.

    According to recent reports, let’s start with Joseph Lochner. Lochner immigrated from Bavaria, Germany, to the United States at the age of 20 in 1882, and settled in Utica, New York. He sought employment in the bakery industry; around 1890, he opened his own small, family bakeshop in Utica.

    According to recent reports, during this time, efforts emerged across New York to regulate the conditions of bakery workers after an article written by Edward Marshall, a muckraker, revealed their unsanitary conditions. In 1895, the state passed The Bakeshop Act, which aimed to prevent biscuit, cake, and bread bakers from working more than 10 hours a day or 60 hours a week.

    Twice charged with violating this statute, Lochner decided to challenge the law on the grounds that it violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause, which he argued protected the economic liberty to enter into such a contract with one’s employees.

    Lochner ultimately made its way to the Supreme Court and presented the court with the question of whether New York’s law violated Lochner’s fundamental liberty interest. Everyone agreed that, under the powers reserved to the states, New York certainly had some powers to regulate general welfare. The question was whether New York had gone too far in restricting an employer’s freedom to contract with his employees.

    For some, the New York statute was perfectly legitimate and a function of the democratic process. As then-future Judge Learned Hand argued, “we should not have the inconsistent spectacle of a government, in theory representative, which distrusted the courage and justice of its representatives, and put its faith in a [judiciary] which was, and ought to be, the least representative of popular feeling." Put simply, if there was a legitimate legislative purpose for the law, then according to Hand, courts should defer to what the elected representatives decided.

    It has been revealed that in what was seen even at the time as a surprising decision, the Supreme Court sided with Lochner five to four. “The general right to make a contract in relation to his business is part of the liberty of the individual protected by the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution,” wrote Justice Rufus Peckham in his majority opinion.

    It has been revealed that while Peckham conceded there could be grounds for the legislature to implement regulations to improve workplace safety, he also held there was not sufficient evidence that the Bakeshop Act’s hour-limits would actually improve worker health. And if the statute was upheld, Peckham argued that it would open up almost every aspect of life to state regulation.

    In dissent, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes lampooned the majority, writing that “a constitution is not intended to embody a particular economic theory.”.

    According to recent reports, lochner has since been abandoned and its reasoning rejected by most legal scholars. Yet defenders remain. Law Professor Randy Barnett, for example, argues for a theory that if the government wants to institute a regulation of liberty, “the burden of proof is more or less on the legislature.” This gets at a fundamental debate in constitutional law: Why do certain civil liberties not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution get heightened scrutiny while economic liberty does not?

    In a recent development, as for Lochner himself, he returned to private life and continued to run his bakery. He died on December 14, 1939.

    Roscoe Filburn: Wickard v. Filburn.

    Few cases are more detested by constitutional conservatives than Wickard v. Filburn. Roscoe Curtiss Filburn was born on August 2, 1902, in Dayton, Ohio. A fifth-generation farmer, Filburn grew crops and raised livestock. The crops included winter wheat, which was, in part, for personal use.

    Recent findings suggest that in a Fresh Deal effort to help prop up the struggling agriculture industry, Congress enacted the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. The secretary of Agriculture would create a national allotment of acres that could be used to produce wheat. The allotment would then be appropriated to states and ultimately to individual farmers. Filburn’s allotment in 1940 was for 11.1 acres of wheat, but he planted 23 acres of it. Administrators of the AAA fined Filburn 49 cents per excess bushel that he grew and placed a lien of $117.11 on his entire wheat yield.

    Filburn challenged the excess penalty in court on the grounds that the statute was passed under the Commerce Clause, which states that Congress shall have the power to “regulate Commerce ... among the several States.” Filburn contended that his activities did not implicate interstate commerce.

    If the winter wheat was grown by Filburn and never crossed state lines, could Congress then regulate it?

    It has been revealed that the Supreme Court sided against Filburn, holding unanimously that his economic activities, taken in the aggregate, would have a substantial effect on interstate commerce. The logic went as follows: If Filburn grew his own wheat, then he would not need to purchase wheat on the open market; and if many farmers did this, it would undermine Congress’ efforts to stabilize the price of crops. “That [Filburn’s] own contribution to the demand for wheat may be trivial by itself is not enough to remove him from the scope of federal regulation where, as here, his contribution, taken together with that of many others similarly situated, is far from trivial,” explained Justice Robert Jackson.

    It has been revealed that the decision remains controversial to this day (to put it mildly). Critics of Filburn argue that the decision gives Congress near unlimited power to enact regulations under the Commerce Clause, effectively allowing Congress to regulate every aspect of people’s lives and largely mooting the powers reserved to the states. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the Supreme Court appeared ready to reduce the Commerce Clause’s reach, striking down two statutes as exceeding Congress’ power. But it has not invalidated a law on these grounds since. (Although the Supreme Court in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius held that Congress lacked the power to enact the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate under the Commerce Clause, it ultimately upheld the mandate under Congress’ power to tax.).

    Industry observers note that filburn returned to private life after his Supreme Court case and rarely spoke about it. During the 1950s, he purchased Beverly Shop, a woman’s beauty store, and, in 1966, Filburn convinced the other successors to his grandparent’s 640-acre farm to collectively sell the land to developers. He died on October 4, 1987, at the age of 85.

    Estelle Griswold: Griswold v. Connecticut.

    Estelle Griswold was born on June 8, 1900, in Hartford, Connecticut. A talented singer, she attended The Hartt School of Music, a music conservatory in Hartford. In 1935, she moved to Washington, D.C. for her husband’s job, where she volunteered at a doctor’s office and worked at George Washington University as a lab instructor.

    In the 1950s, Griswold moved to Latest Haven and a few years later was offered the role of executive director of the Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut. In 1961, she opened a birth control clinic in New Haven, along with a doctor, but was convicted and fined $100 in violation of the Barnum Act, a Connecticut law that prohibited the use of “any drug, medicine, article, or instrument” to prevent conception (and, yes, named after that Barnum).

    In a recent development, griswold challenged her conviction on the grounds that the Barnum Act was unconstitutional. As some of the act’s legal defenders pointed out, although many may regard such a law as a profound violation of personal autonomy, the Constitution lacks any mention of “privacy,” never mind preventative contraception. Put succinctly by Justice Potter Stewart in his dissenting opinion, “I can find no such general right of privacy in the Bill of Rights, in any other part of the Constitution, or in any case ever before decided by this Court.” (To be fair, the idea of the Constitution containing a right to privacy was not fresh when Griswold was decided; albeit in a different context, Justice Louis Brandeis had articulated such a right in an 1890 law review article.).

    In a 7-2 decision, the Supreme Court found the Barnum Act unconstitutional and held that married couples have a right to contraception as part of an implicit right to privacy. Justice William Douglas contended that the lack of its enumeration does not preclude that right from existing under the Constitution, akin to precedent in which the court found a parental right to send their children to religious schools. According to Douglas, “specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance. ... Various guarantees create zones of privacy.”.

    While Douglas’ vote for a constitutional right to privacy won the day, his articulation of penumbras and emanations did not fare so well (although Justice Clarence Thomas apparently still pays “tribute” to this language with a sign in his office reading “Please do not emanate into the penumbra”). Rather, concurring in the judgement, Justice John Harlan II argued that the “teachings of history [and] solid recognition of the basic values that underlie our society” based in the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause supported the decision in Griswold, a standard that has since become the prevailing defense of the right to privacy and served as a foundation for later Supreme Court decisions such as Roe v. Wade and Obergefell v. Hodges.

    Soon after the decision was confirmed, the PPLC clinic reopened, but Griswold stepped down as executive director as she had fallen out of favor with some members of the organization due to its continued financial struggles. Griswold passed away on August 13, 1981, in Fort Myers, Florida at age 81 and was posthumously inducted into the Connecticut Women’s Hall of Fame in 1994.

    The Tinkers: Tinker v. Des Moines.

    According to recent reports, another major area of constitutional controversy has involved the limits of free speech in the classroom context. Although such cases continue to crop up (BONG HiTS 4 JESUS, anyone?), the modern foundation for them was laid in 1969’s Tinker v. Des Moines. Which brings us to the Tinkers.

    John Tinker was born in 1950, and his sister, Mary Beth, was born in 1952. They grew up in Atlantic, Iowa, where their father was the pastor of a Methodist church. In November 1965, John, then a high schooler, attended a rally in opposition to the Vietnam War in Washington, D.C. On the way back to Iowa, John and other protesters agreed to wear black armbands to protest the war and to mourn the deaths on both sides.

    According to recent reports, more than 50 students across public schools in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to school on December 16, 1965, in support of Sen. Robert Kennedy’s proposed Christmas truce. However, local principals instituted a policy that all students wearing black armbands would be asked to remove them.

    In a recent development, on December 16, 1965, Mary Beth wore a black armband to Warren Harding Junior High School and was suspended after she refused to take it off. The next day, John wore a black armband to North High School and was also suspended after declining to remove it.

    In March 1966, the Tinkers sued, arguing the schools violated their constitutional rights. Specifically, the Tinkers contended that the public schools were an arm of the state and they were therefore bound by the First Amendment.

    According to recent reports, allan Herrick, arguing for Des Moines at the Supreme Court, contended that the school district must be in a position to “preserve order and to avoid this disturbance and disruption in the school room.” As Justice Thomas would argue decades later in Morse v. Frederick, “through the legal doctrine of in loco parentis [in the place of a parent], courts [historically] upheld the right of schools to discipline students, to enforce rules, and to maintain order.”.

    It has been revealed that in February 1969, the Supreme Court sided with the Tinkers, holding that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” In its decision, written by Justice Abe Fortas, the court established the substantial disruption test, which sets the necessary conditions for regulating student speech. To do so, the school must be able to reasonably foretell “material and substantial interference” with other students’ learning or the school’s operations. Fortas held that the school district failed to show that the Tinkers’ protests resulted in any material disruption.

    Sources indicate that to this day, Tinker receives mixed reviews. Supporters of an expansive interpretation of the First Amendment tend to support the principles in Tinker and argue that they should be even more broadly applied; critics, such as Justice Thomas, are skeptical that students have First Amendment rights at all. (As Justice Hugo Black put it in his Tinker dissent, “It may be that the Nation has outworn the old-fashioned slogan that ‘children are to be seen, not heard,’ but one may, I hope, be permitted to harbor the thought that taxpayers send children to school on the premise that, at their age, they need to learn, not teach.”).

    After the Supreme Court’s decision, John Tinker remained active in anti-Vietnam war demonstrations and later became the manager of KPIP-LP 94.7 FM, a local radio station, which he manages to this day. Mary Beth Tinker pursued a career in medicine, working as a pediatric and emergency room nurse and a nurse practitioner. In 2013, Mary Beth left the nursing field and embarked on the “Tinker Tour,” where she travels the country telling her story and promoting civic education to young people.

    Clarence Brandenburg: Brandenburg v. Ohio.

    Let’s conclude with our least likable plaintiff, who nevertheless established one of the most enduring Supreme Court precedents. Clarence Brandenburg was born on March 3, 1916, in Lee County, Kentucky. A Marine Corps veteran, he worked at a General Electric plant and operated a television repair shop upon returning to civilian life. After declaring personal bankruptcy in 1959, Brandenburg began getting involved with white supremacist organizations and sought to become a leader of the KKK.

    In a recent development, in June 1964, Brandenburg spoke at a Klan rally, which was shown on a local television station. Brandenburg remarked “We're not a revengent organization, but if our President, our Congress, our Supreme Court, continues to suppress the white, Caucasian race, it's possible that there might have to be some revengeance taken. ... We are marching on Congress July the Fourth, four hundred thousand strong.” He was then charged with violating Ohio’s criminal syndicalism statute prohibiting advocating “sabotage, violence, or ... terrorism ... as a means of accomplishing ... political reform,” and later convicted.

    Industry observers note that brandenburg appealed, arguing that his speech was protected by the First Amendment. Specifically, he argued that Ohio could not punish him for advocating for unlawful action without showing that his speech was directed towards producing such action.

    Recent findings suggest that leonard Kirschner, arguing on behalf of Ohio at the Supreme Court, asserted that Brandenburg’s actions were not conducted in isolation and could lead to violence, contending that “the statements [made by Brandenburg] to 10 or 20 people can cause one heck of a lot of crime and violence and terrorism in any community. It only takes one person to cause it.”.

    The Supreme Court reversed Brandenburg’s conviction in 1969 on First Amendment grounds. According to the court, the Ohio statute in question failed to distinguish between an abstract endorsement of unlawful activity and speech directed towards producing imminent, lawless action. In doing so, the court established what became known as the Brandenburg test, which required that speech sufficient for incitement be “directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action” and “likely to incite or produce such action.”.

    In 1971, Brandenburg was found guilty of harassing his Jewish neighbor by repeatedly calling him and uttering antisemitic slurs. He died on March 29, 1986.

    According to recent reports, they came from different backgrounds, had very different worldviews, and dealt with different issues, but each of these plaintiffs had one thing in common: pushing up against the limits of state power. How that power manifested itself differed considerably, as did the court’s willingness to reign it in. For example, while the court has advanced a highly protective understanding of the First Amendment, it has been more hesitant to advance protections of economic liberty.

    Recent findings suggest that the nature of the plaintiff also mattered less in these cases than one might presume. Filburn was a farmer who grew wheat for his own personal consumption but did not prevail at the court. Brandenburg, on the other hand, expressed white supremacist ideas yet proved successful before the justices, becoming responsible for an entirely upcoming free speech doctrine.

    Some may view the court blinding itself to the actual facts on the ground as too simplistic; others as an ideal to aspire to. On that note, we’ll give Justice Elena Kagan the final word: “the question is not do you like this party or do you like that party ... the question is what the law requires.”.

    Blake Fox is an intern for SCOTUSblog.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has instituted a rule requiring mandatory human review of all court filings that use artificial intelligence. (Photo by Getty Images).

    In an unprecedented move, a U.S. federal appeals court has instituted a rule requiring mandatory human review of all court filings that use artificial intelligence.

    The 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver posted a newly introduced rule Friday stipulating attorneys and pro see parties certify human verification of all cited authorities and quotations, Law360 reports.

    Recent findings suggest that at the start of next year, the 10th Circuit can address violations by waiving the affected glitch, striking a noncompliant document or affirming or dismissing an appeal. The judge may also impose monetary sanctions or demand coverage of some of the opponent’s attorney fees.

    Industry observers note that four years after generative AI debuted on a mass scale, many fake citations have been discovered in court filings resulting from large language models sometimes producing false information or hallucinations, according to Law360. French data consultant Damien Charlotin found that court cases involving hallucinated case citations worldwide have decreased this year, which he attributes to hallucination awareness and LLM improvements.

    #216037. Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2009 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that when the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court.
    • Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners.
    • According to recent reports, the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that when the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

    Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom, Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook, which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

    According to recent reports, the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.

    The prior article in this series examined how frequently the Trump and Biden administrations prevailed. In turning to the individual justices, I reviewed federal executive-action decisions from 2017 through November 12, 2026, consolidated into 106 distinct substantive decisions. The three administrations account for 32, 36, and 38 decisions, respectively.

    According to recent reports, there is a very notable qualification throughout: the court often publishes emergency orders without identifying each justice’s vote. The analysis thus assigned a justice to the court’s majority ruling when they were silent, absent an express position or other evidence indicating otherwise.

    So what can we say about the different justices’ support for the Trump administration on the emergency docket?

    Different presidents, different justices.

    Recent findings suggest that the most consistent record belongs to Roberts. He aligned with federal executive positions in 23 of 31 eligible decisions during Trump’s first administration, 26 of 36 under Biden, and 28 of 38 during Trump’s second administration. Those figures amount to 74%, 72%, and 74%. The disputes changed markedly, but Roberts’ aggregate willingness to leave the federal government’s position intact – or grant it relief – barely moved. In other words, Roberts has typically supported executive power on the emergency docket regardless of who is president.

    The next most consistent justice, Barrett (though with a much lower sample size), aligned with Biden in 69% of her eligible decisions and Trump II in 78%. Third was Kavanaugh, with rates of 78%, 67%, and 79%. Then came Gorsuch, with rates of 83%, 54%, and 84%.

    Thomas and Alito present a very different picture. Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II. Alito’s corresponding figures were 83%, 47%, and 92%.

    Industry observers note that the liberal justices show the opposite movement, although their individual records differ. Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II. Sotomayor’s rates were 27%, 94%, and 16%. Jackson, who joined the court during Biden’s presidency, supported its executive position in 21 of 24 eligible decisions (88%), compared with three of 38 (8%) under Trump II.

    Industry observers note that the figure above makes these distinctions particularly clear. Roberts remains between 72% and 74% across the three periods, while Thomas’ support moves from 83% under Trump I to 39% under Biden and 92% under Trump II. The middle group of Barrett, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch is more varied, but each supported Biden’s executive position more frequently than a simple Republican-versus-Democratic framing might suggest.

    These numbers are telling, but they do not establish the reasons for why the justices decided as they did. For example, a president defending an environmental rule presents a very different legal issue from one seeking permission to remove an independent agency official. To determine how much of the observed variation is associated with presidential identity, the next step is to examine the kinds of cases that produced it.

    The issues that unite and divide the justices.

    Immigration provides a useful point of comparison because it generated substantial emergency litigation under all three administrations. Roberts supported the executive in 10 of 11 immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and 11 of 13 under Trump II. Thomas supported the government in 10 of 10 eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and 12 of 13 under Trump II. Kagan’s comparable figures were six of eleven, six of six, and five of 13.

    This is revealing. Roberts and Thomas both supported Trump’s immigration positions at high rates but not as much when Biden defended his administration’s policies. Kagan and Sotomayor supported Biden in all six coded immigration decisions, then opposed most of Trump II positions. But there is, of course, a key caveat: This category covers different immigration rules, as opposed to simple support for one president over another.

    Public-health and related health litigation under Biden revealed a sharper division within the conservative majority. In 10 eligible health-coded decisions, Roberts and Kavanaugh each supported the federal executive in seven, compared with one each for Thomas and Alito. Barrett supported it in five; Gorsuch in two. Kagan and Sotomayor each supported the government in nine such cases. (Jackson’s two favorable positions came from only three eligible decisions in this category, making her figure much less informative.).

    Industry observers note that the court’s January 2022 vaccination decisions supply a concrete example. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in allowing the administration to enforce a vaccination requirement for workers at healthcare facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid funding, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. On the same day, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the conservatives in blocking OSHA’s broader vaccination-or-testing standard. To Roberts and Kavanaugh, health litigation was clearly treated issue-by-issue.

    In a recent development, let’s move on to personnel decisions, or the president’s control over the executive branch. In the nine Trump II personnel and removal decisions, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett supported the executive in eight, while Roberts and Kavanaugh did so in seven. In four foreign-affairs and national-security decisions, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch aligned with the government in all of these, compared with two for Roberts and Barrett.

    According to recent reports, subject matter therefore helps explain how things break down. The same conservative justice may support emergency intervention in a dispute over immigration enforcement while resisting it in a case involving agency regulation. The legal authority being asserted, the posture of the case, and the requested remedy all shape the decision.

    The coalitions inside the conservative majority.

    According to recent reports, so which justices most frequently aligned? At the front of the pack are Thomas and Alito, who agreed in all 38 coded Trump II decisions. Their alignment is particularly visible when the administration lost. In seven events, both of their positions favored more relief for the administration than the majority granted or would otherwise provide.

    Recent findings suggest that other pairings are almost as cohesive. Roberts and Barrett agreed in 35 of 36 Trump II decisions (97%). Roberts and Kavanaugh agreed in 36 of 38 of these (95%), as did Gorsuch and Kavanaugh. The next figure displays those pairings alongside the liberal and cross-ideological relationships. The high agreement rates show how often the conservatives arrive at the same apparent disposition, but the exceptions reveal competing views about the scope of emergency judicial intervention.

    The foreign-assistance dispute in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, for instance, separated Roberts and Barrett from Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh. The four dissenters would have granted the administration relief from an order requiring payment for foreign-aid work already completed. Roberts and Barrett did not join that position. Their disagreement concerned what a district court could require of the government while the underlying funding litigation continued.

    It has been revealed that A different alignment emerged in NIH v. American Public Health Association. There, the court granted partial relief in litigation over terminated research grants. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh would have granted the administration’s request in full, while Roberts joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson in seeking to deny it altogether. Barrett supported an intermediate outcome.

    In Cook, the division shifted again. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in rejecting the administration’s attempt to immediately remove a Federal Reserve governor, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. In Trump v. Illinois, concerning the Trump administration’s deployment of National Guard forces, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch disagreed with the court’s denial of relief to Trump, while Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds.

    It has been revealed that the evidence points toward distinctive approaches to removal authority, spending, the judicial supervision of agencies, and emergency remedies. Justices who agree in one field can diverge in another, and partial orders sometimes put a justice between two groups seeking opposing forms of relief.

    The liberal justices and the unusual alliances across ideological lines.

    Industry observers note that the three liberal justices also exhibited some meaningful disagreements. Under Trump II, Jackson aligned with the executive in only three of 38 emergency decisions (8%), compared with six for Sotomayor (16%) and nine for Kagan (24%). Kagan and Sotomayor agreed in 35 of 38 such decisions; Kagan and Jackson in 32. The differences are not as dramatic as those dividing the conservatives, but they complicate the assumption that the liberal trio behaves as a single bloc in every emergency dispute.

    Their publicly registered dissents differ as well. Jackson expressly opposed a Trump II executive position in 26 decisions, Sotomayor in 23, and Kagan in 20. In FCC v. Brown, for example, Sotomayor and Jackson publicly indicated that they would deny the agency’s stay application, while Kagan registered no public disagreement.

    Trump’s second term has produced more than one identifiable cross-ideological alignment. The five-justice majority in Cook included Roberts, Kavanaugh, and the three liberals, while the NIH grants dispute placed Roberts and the liberals together against complete relief. Barrett also joined certain portions of Sotomayor’s dissent in Trump v. J.G.G., a dispute involving the Alien Enemies Act, although her partial join should not necessarily be counted as agreement with the liberals on the case.

    These examples again highlight why the distinction between shared results and shared legal reasoning is crucial. A justice can favor the same outcome as an ideological opponent while arriving there for entirely different reasons (we see this with concurrences in merits cases all the time). Separate opinions can also reveal agreement on a particular procedural or statutory question even when the justices disagree on the ultimate relief. At the same time, the emergency docket makes these relationships especially difficult to measure comprehensively because many orders contain no individual vote information at all.

    My analysis of the emergency docket shows a chief most reluctant to favor one administration over another, with Barrett and Kavanaugh following closely behind; Gorsuch acting more favorably towards the Trump administration, although not overwhelmingly so; Thomas and Alito disproportionately favoring Trump over Biden; and the three liberal justices acting as a near mirror image of Thomas and Alito – although to varied degrees.

    We thus see a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.

    Sources indicate that dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

    #216033. Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2116 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that american exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself.
    • According to recent reports, at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result.
    • It has been revealed that and then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that american exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of Latest England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us.”.

    According to recent reports, at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the Latest England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Blueprint, the World Bank, and the presently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment, the juvenile death penalty (until 2005), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

    It has been revealed that and then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law.

    In a recent development, A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, in which the justices will review one of the Trump administration’s earliest attempts to restrict immigration. On the administration’s first day, a presidential proclamation declared that “an invasion is ongoing on the southern border.” The proclamation, among other things, sought to suspend entry to the United States for non-citizens “engaged in the invasion,” even for refugees fleeing persecution and seeking to apply for asylum. But the edict went one step further. It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.

    The proclamation was issued notwithstanding a congressional framework that seeks to facilitate asylum – indefinite lawful residence – to those escaping persecution in their home country, set forth primarily in the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by the 1980 Refugee Act and later amendments (codified under Title 8 of the U.S. Code). This framework: a) ensures a right to apply for asylum, b) links eligibility for asylum to refugee status, and c) provides protections against the government removing persons who would be likely to face persecution or torture.

    Sources indicate that section 1158 establishes the right to seek asylum. It provides that “[a]ny alien who is physically present in the United States … irrespective of such alien’s status, may apply for asylum.” The same section makes eligibility for asylum conditional, among other things, on a demonstration of refugee status. For this the statute relies on the definition of refugee in section 1101(a)(42) as a person who is unwilling or unable to return to their home country “because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”.

    In a recent development, in turn, safeguards from removal come from two sources. The immigration statute itself states that noncitizens cannot be removed to a country where the attorney general determines that the “alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” In addition, the Foreign Affairs Reform & Restructuring Act of 1998 restricts removal to a country when “there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.”.

    The Trump administration initially justified the denial of asylum and removal protections to those within the United States by invoking the president’s authority to suspend entry “of any aliens or of any class of aliens into the United States [that] would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The logic is that no one who violated the suspension by entering should be entitled to asylum and removal protections. To this defense the administration has added the formal role of the attorney general and director of Homeland Security. The INA grants each official the authority to grant asylum to eligible applicants as well as withhold removal for those who qualify. At the same time, the statute makes clear that these decisions are subject to individualized judicial review under an “abuse of discretion” standard. (At least until the second Trump administration, decisions not to grant relief to those who had demonstrated that they had qualified for asylum were the “exceedingly rare“ exception.).

    In a recent development, the lower courts rejected both justifications. Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the administration’s claim that the president’s suspension of entry to those “engaged in [the] invasion” invalidated asylum and removal protections that expressly applied to persons physically in the country. The D.C. Circuit agreed with a slightly different emphasis. Writing for the majority, Judge Michelle Childs also rejected the idea that a suspension of entry justified eliminating asylum and removal safeguards for those present in the United States. To this point she added that, as a grant of asylum is discretionary, the express right to apply it entails individualized consideration rather than blanket elimination. (Judge Justin Walker issued a partial dissenting argument that the grant of discretionary authority permits a blanket denial of asylum claims.).

    The D.C. courts’ holdings are not wrong so far as they go. Suspending entry would appear to be a different power from removing someone after they had entered. The provisions for asylum strongly imply individualized consideration and even suggest a presumption of granting asylum to those who meet the detailed eligibility requirements. The relevant provisions plainly bar removal of those who qualify for that protection. But whether this reasoning will be sufficient at the Supreme Court is another matter. This is so not least given the justices’ recent penchant for giving the executive wide latitude on immigration.

    But the justices should take into account some additional perspective.

    Industry observers note that one relevant perspective comes from international law. Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum. More surprising still, these common global challenges has yielded what should be familiar, common legal standards that apply, and to a great extent which owe their development to, the United States. Perhaps most surprising of all, standard domestic doctrines invite reference to this body of law when interpreting applicable federal statutes.

    Consider first asylum. As an initial matter, the domestic asylum framework incorporates international standards as a function of congressional intent. As the court itself recognized in 1987’s INS v. Cardozo-Fonseca, Congress enacted the Refugee Act of 1980 to bring U.S. law in conformity with the nation’s obligations as a state party to the 1967 Protocol to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Crucially, in determining those obligations, the court sensibly drew upon the views of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees.

    Sources indicate that what do those obligations contemplate? The Refugee Conventions do not expressly provide for a right to apply for long-term asylum, as opposed to specifying rights for refugees fleeing persecution. But the UNCHR has maintained that international law presupposes individualized consideration of refugee status, especially before that status is denied. Given that Congress made the requirements for refugee status the basis for being eligible for asylum, it would be odd to conclude that the U.S. would remain in conformity with the convention as interpreted by the UN’s most authoritative body should the executive reject the right to seek asylum by means of a categorial denial of all asylum claims.

    According to recent reports, not surprisingly, categorical rejection of asylum claims would also be at variance with widespread international practice, especially as mandated in Europe. And neither last nor least, the administration’s position would also be inconsistent with the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ express guarantee of a right to asylum. Though not binding, the UDHR was adopted without dissent by the UN General Assembly, reflects the dominant position of the Member States, and informs their practice.

    Sources indicate that the Charming Betsy canon leads to the same conclusion. In the 1804 case Murray v. the Schooner Charming Betsy, Chief Justice John Marshall famously stated that “an act of Congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations if any other possible construction remains.” Marshall’s reference to the “law of nations” is generally understood to apply to modern customary international law. International custom arises given a near consensus of state practice perused out of a sense of legal obligation.

    Section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways. It might mean a complete categorical discretion to deny. Or it might be better understood to assume individualized consideration. The latter clearly better comports with international practice. Yet there is even a stronger consideration. Customary, and for that matter treaty law, clearly prohibits removal to countries where a refugee has a well-founded fear of facing persecution or torture. When the result is expedited removal, the categorical denial of asylum status to persons claiming to escape from persecution and torture places the U.S. in obvious jeopardy of violating exactly this well-established international prohibition.

    Recent findings suggest that which brings up the matter of removal itself. Here the upshot of Congress’ intent is more direct. Article 33.1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention provides: “No Contracting State shall expel or return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” Likewise, Article 3.1 of the Convention Against Torture mandates that “No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” As noted, the Refugee Act in the first instance sought to place the U.S. in conformity with the Refugee Convention. FARRA sought to do the same with CAT. Categorically removing persons in the U.S. seeking asylum all but guarantees violations of the treaties that Congress sought to uphold.

    Sources indicate that so strong is the congressional intent argument that the Charming Betsy need not set sail. Yet even if the relevant statutory provisions were somehow ambiguous, the Charming Betsy canon would compel rejection of the administration’s position. Assume that section 1182(f), which grants the executive discretion to deny asylum claims, authorizes a categorial denial of applications across the board. Assume further that this section, along with section 1185(a)(1), can be read to permit removal of persons within the United States denied the opportunity to apply for asylum on the basis of persecution or torture. Even without the conventions, international practice has separately established “non-refoulement” – the prohibition of returning, or “refouling,” a person to return to a territory where he may be exposed to persecution as a matter of binding customary international law. Reading the relevant statutes to permit removal would then constitute a clear violation of non-refoulement. That reading would therefore also run counter to the Charming Betsy canon.

    A sad yet likely irony is that Mullin v. RAICES will privilege one strand of American exceptionalism over another. Much of the international law relevant to the case reflects the nation’s exceptional effort to leverage its dominance after the Second World War not to establish a traditional empire, but to construct a rules-based international order. One of many achievements was the 1951 Refugee Convention, like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, brought about in no small part thanks to the efforts of Eleanor Roosevelt as a U.S. representative to the UN. Against this is the view that America has little to heed from the rest of the world, including on matters that implicate international affairs. The court adopted this stance on immigration as recently as last term. We shall see which view prevails.

    Martin Flaherty is Charles and Marie Robertson Visiting Professor at the School of Public and International Affairs at Princeton, and Leitner Family Professor Chair of International Human Rights Law at Fordham Law School in Upcoming York.

    Recommended Citation: Martin Flaherty, Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 24, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/refugees-asylum-and-supreme-court-exceptionalism/.

    #216032. California sees record high tides, but limited damage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (509 w)

    California sees record high tides, but limited damage

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Courthousenews

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The king tides caused massive waves, but little more than minor flooding.
    • (CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.
    • Preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The king tides caused massive waves, but little more than minor flooding.

    (CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.

    Preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923. La Jolla and Santa Barbara had all-time record high tides, though the data for Santa Barbara only goes as far back as 1990.

    State and local officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, had warned extensive flooding could disrupt travel prepares and flood coastal communities. Those fears appear not to have been fully realized.

    Todd Hall, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office in Oxnard, noted two factors prevented the tides from being worse: Storm surge in Northern California petered out, and the high tide and large swells happened independently.

    “There is some reprieve, because the high tide this morning, surf and swell coming up into tonight,” Hall said. “Things would be much worse if we had high surf arriving at the same time we had high tide.”.

    Some areas did see minor flooding. Streets were underwater in the low-lying neighborhood of Sunset Beach in Huntington Beach this morning. Meanwhile, in the Bay Area, water from San Francisco Bay spilled onto the Embarcadero, and in Pacifica massive waves destroyed a section of the municipal pier. Santa Cruz County and Marin County both issued evacuation warnings for homes along the coast, though the latter has already been lifted.

    Warnings and advisories remain in place up and down the coast, but so far, the king tides have been less destructive than feared.

    It has been revealed that “It is a relief, that things weren’t worse,” said Febe Rothenberg, meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Francisco. Still, she warned: “Pretty please, avoid the beach.”.

    It has been revealed that king tides, also called perigean spring tides, are predictable astronomical events that occur when a newly introduced or full moon lines up with both the sun and Earth. The gravitational pull of the three bodies combine and cause exceptionally high tides. The next king tide will be a month from now, on Christmas Eve, when tides could be even higher if a storm hits.

    This year’s especially strong El NiÃ±o means unusually warm surface waters in the Pacific Ocean, with higher-than-average tides, larger waves and more frequent storms.

    Scientists predict tides will be higher and higher because of global warming, which has melted glaciers and caused ocean levels to rise 3-4 inches in the last 30 years.

    When Michael Moritz donated more than $30 million to Ohio State University’s law school in 2001, he expected that the money would fund four faculty chairs and 30 annual law school scholarships.

    It has been revealed that but despite that agreement, records from the law school renamed after him show that the fund inexplicably fell from $30 million to $21.9 in less than 15 years, his son Jeffrey Mortiz writes in the Columbus Dispatch. Only 12 to 15 scholarships have been provided annually, he adds.

    It has been revealed that in the column, Moritz called upon the Ohio legislature to fix this by passing the Endowment Accountability Act, House Bill 751 and Senate Bill 368 by the end of December. The bill states that donors who believe a public university has violated an endowment agreement must first notify the state’s attorney general, who has 180 days to correct course. Donors in Ohio now have no clear way to hold public universities accountable.

    According to recent reports, A former head of Baker & Hostetler’s corporate practice and director of Cardinal Health, Michael Moritz attended Ohio State’s law school on a full-ride scholarship before graduating in 1958. Less than a year after making his donation, Moritz, 68, was killed by a hit-and-run driver in Naples, Florida.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I dedicate my Thanksgiving column each year to the Indian Nation from whom I learned so much, the Tohono Oâodham, with whom I spent six of the best years of my life.

    I taught English, music and journalism and coached distance runners on the second-largest Indian reservation in the United States. The Oâodham are the only Indian Nation that never was at war with the United States and never were removed from their homelands.

    And I bet youâve never heard of them.

    The reason they never were at daggers drawn with Uncle Sam is that the Oâodham were a sedentary, transhumant agricultural tribe whose perennial enemies were the Apache.

    Transhumant means the quasi-sedentary people moved regularly from one climate zone to another, then returned: highlands in the summer, when itâs so hot on the desert floor, and you can hunt animals on the mountains, then back to the desert when the rains came, to harvest beans and squash.

    In Oâodham itâs called ak chin farming: farming at the mouth of the wash.

    Sources indicate that A wash is a dry riverbed. You can see them all over what we call southern Arizona. The only time thereâs water in a wash is right after a monsoon rain. Mark Twain stated he fell into a desert river once, âand came up all dusty.â.

    On the year I moved to the rez to teach at Baboquivari High School, I had an average of 43 students in my three English classes, and no desks for students, only the one for me.

    Fortunately, or not, it was the band room, so my students shared music stands to write out my assignments.

    Fortunately, or not, the ceiling was falling down, and, stashed in a closet, with a jumble of battered horns â all of our horns were battered â a kindly janitor had left us half a gallon of ceiling plaster. Which I used to patch up the pads on the flutes, saxophones and clarinets.

    Thatâs how it was on the rez when I got there. All but forgotten by Uncle Sam. And in some ways, good riddance to our uncle. But not so good that our uncle wouldnât buy desks for the only public school on the 3-million-acre reservation: twice the size of Delaware.

    Well, you do what you can, and you do what you must.

    It has been revealed that I dug life on the rez. Learning stuff I never knew I didnât know. Tryna pick up the language, and man, thatâs a tough language to learn. About all thatâs stuck with me is, âAyy, jum skug!â.

    Jum skug, as I understand it, means someone is âtrying to act.â Like a big shot.

    Industry observers note that I tried not to be jum skug. Still try not to.

    I loved those years on the rez. Those 2,200 days.

    In a recent development, hereâs another thing I learned. Iâll bet youâve been in this situation: Youâre in a party of mostly white people (mirgan); conversations are bubbling along in a crowded room, then all at once, the room is silent. Two, four seconds pass, then someone states something, probably stupid, just to *break the silence.*People laugh, and the party continues.

    Itâs like the mirgan canât stand silence in a room.

    Iâve been in rooms with Oâodham where that silence continues, and no one feels that itâs necessary to break the silence. When someone finally speaks, itâs because sheâs got something to say â itâs not because she canât stand silence.

    Thereâs nothing wrong with silence.

    Here are some other things I learned on the rez.

    If you donât know what to say, shut up.

    If youâre not sure of what you want to say, shut up.

    If youâre called upon to speak, but donât know what you want to say, or donât know much about the subject: shut up.

    In celebration of Thanksgiving today (Thorâs Day), Iâd like to address all 535 members of Congress, and all of their appointed staffs, all the appointed members of the executive branch, and all the appointed, paid-off, cushy and cowardly members of our Supreme Court: to all of them, and to so many more, in our federal and state houses around the nation, Iâd like to tell yâall what I learned on the rez:.

    If you donât know what youâre talking about, shut the fuck up.

    #216024. Breaking: Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (485 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.
    • According to recent reports, the skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case.
    • It has been revealed that lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order, which came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case, indicated that the justices would instead “defer[]” that ruling “pending oral argument,” which is scheduled for Wednesday, December 2.

    According to recent reports, the skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case. Viramontes, who has been part of the challenge since it was filed in 2021, did not provide any explanation for his request.

    It has been revealed that lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue. They emphasized that Viramontes was a Cook County resident who noted that he wanted to own an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle. By contrast, they wrote, the other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, has said that he wants to own “an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle,” which, according to Cook County, is not the kind of AR-15-style rifle covered by the question before the court.

    According to recent reports, the challengers countered that the question presented is not limited to AR-15 rifles but also extends to “similar” semiautomatic rifles, which would include AK-47-style rifles like the IMI Galil. But in any event, they added, Khaya “also desires to possess an AR-15 platform rifle and would acquire one if it were lawful for him to do so.”.

    Industry observers note that in its order deferring a decision on whether the Cook County case is moot because of the dismissal of Viramontes from the case, the Supreme Court cited its 2023 decision in Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, in which it unanimously agreed after oral argument that the case was moot because the plaintiff had voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit in the lower court. But the chances that the court will ultimately reach the merits of the ban are likely higher than in Acheson, in which there was only one plaintiff, because the dispute over semiautomatic rifles encompasses not only multiple plaintiffs but also another case – a challenge to Connecticut’s ban on AR-15-style rifles.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, europe fast-tracked renewable energy permits after Russian gas supplies fell. A Belgian case tested how much discretion local officials still had under those rules.

    (CN) â The Belgian region Wallonia mentioned no to two wind turbines near its capital to protect the views, but the EUâs top court ruled Thursday that even scenery could take a back seat to qualifying renewable projects under the blocâs emergency rules.

    Eneco Wind Belgium asked the national Council of State to overturn the Walloon regionâs refusal to let it build and operate the turbines in Andoy, on the outskirts of Namur. The company argued officials had overlooked the priority its project should receive underÂ an emergency EU rule. The Belgian judgesÂ asked the Court of Justice of the European Union how far that rule could go.

    In a recent development, eneco filed for its permit in April 2023, a few months after the EU moved to speed up renewable energy construction. Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine and cuts in Russian gas supplies had sent energy prices soaring. Getting wind and other renewable projects online faster offered a way to replace some of that fuel.

    In a recent development, in Andoy, the prepares called for access roads, a substation and underground cables. A public inquiry drew complaints, and Walloon officials turned down the project that October, citing the areaâs landscape and heritage. Officials reviewing Enecoâs appeal recommended a permit with conditions. The ministers handling the appeal missed the deadline to notify Eneco of a decision, so the refusal stood.

    According to recent reports, the EU judgesÂ saidÂ projects recognized as serving an overriding public interest had to get priority even when the competing concern fell outside EU rules on birds, habitats and waterways. Limiting that advantage to those environmental laws, they reasoned, would blunt a measure designed to speed up permitting.

    In a recent development, for Hendrik Schoukens, a professor of environmental law at Ghent University, the ruling narrowed officialsâ discretion in an area where governments set their own standards. âThis is important, since landscape protection is not a harmonized interest by EU law,â he noted.

    In a recent development, officials could still put a competing interest first if they gave reasons specific to the project. The judges pointed to the ruleâs instruction to weigh those interests case by case. âThat provision would be devoid of purpose if the priority of those projects were to arise automatically from the mere recognition of their being of overriding public interest,â the court wrote.

    In a recent development, for projects that needed an exception to EU bird or habitat protections, there was still the question of whether they could go ahead another way. Harm Dotinga, a senior legal adviser on nature protection at BirdLife Netherlands, noted a well-supported refusal could still protect biodiversity. He pointed to separate legal requirements, including the need to show there was no satisfactory alternative. âThose may also justify rejection of the project if properly motivated,â he said. Schoukens said it was striking how little attention the Belgian proceedings had paid to alternatives, given that a more sustainable option could still sink a project.

    Whether a project qualified for priority in the first place depended on what stood in its way. Officials could rely on an existing presumption that it served an overriding public interest, including where national law extended that presumption to landscape protection. Where the presumption did not apply or was called into question, the project needed formal recognition.

    Recent findings suggest that eline Dhaen, a spokesperson for Eneco Belgium, said the company was reviewing the ruling. The Walloon Region did not respond to a request for comment.

    A permit with conditions, as officials had recommended in Andoy, was another option. The court remarked authorities could require developers to limit or make up for environmental damage and, where the law allowed, let some measures follow approval. Where species protection was at stake, the priority rule required conservation measures backed by sufficient funding and land.

    Elisa Cristea, a senior associate specializing in energy and environmental law at Romanian firm Èuca ZbÃ¢rcea & AsociaÈii, welcomed the ruling and saw conditional permits as its most practical point.

    âThis reflects a shift in the approach to permitting: Authorities should consider how competing interests can be accommodated rather than treating them solely as grounds for refusing a project,â she stated.

    Cristea said the judges left officials more leeway than Advocate General Athanasios Rantos, who had proposed that departures from the priority rule be exceptional and backed by a detailed assessment. She said the ruling could outlast the expired emergency measure if EU lawmakers adoptedÂ a European Commission proposalÂ to restore priority over a wider range of competing interests.

    Industry observers note that thursdayâs ruling is binding and cannot be appealed. Belgiumâs Council of State now has to apply it to the question still open in Andoy: whether Walloniaâs refusal stands.

    • (AFP) â A trade deal struck last week between Britain and the EU as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s reset with the bloc contains a termination clause, London confirmed Thursday.
    • It comes as the leaders of the right-wing opposition Conservative and Reform UK parties suggested they could seek to scrap the agreements if they defeat Labour at the next general election.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It includes a clause meaning that if one party ends the agreement within its first 10 years they would have to pay to rebuild the border checks infrastructure that the deal removes.

    (AFP) â A trade deal struck last week between Britain and the EU as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s reset with the bloc contains a termination clause, London confirmed Thursday.

    It comes as the leaders of the right-wing opposition Conservative and Reform UK parties suggested they could seek to scrap the agreements if they defeat Labour at the next general election.

    Burnham has reignited the Brexit wars that dominated political discourse following the narrow victory for the leave campaign during the 2016 referendum by suggesting Britain could apply to rejoin one day.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.K. premier and top EU officials signed three agreements in Brussels on Nov. 20 designed to improve post-Brexit ties in the short-term, kicking decisions on their long-term relationship down the road.

    They include the so-called sanitary and phytosanitary deal, which the British government says could add 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7 billion) to the country’s economy by slashing red tape on food and drink exports.

    It includes a clause meaning that if one party ends the agreement within its first 10 years they would have to pay to rebuild the border checks infrastructure that the deal removes.

    “That termination clause is a standard practice in international treaties, and this one applies equally to both sides, including the EU,” Burnham’s deputy spokesperson told reporters.

    U.K. officials remarked an upfront sum for breaking the deal had not been stipulated.

    An EU diplomat told AFP that the reciprocal clause “provides stability for the agreement to deliver its benefits.”.

    Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think tank, said it “makes sense” for the EU given the ongoing debate in Britain about its future relations with Brussels.

    “It’s an insurance policy,” he told AFP.

    Friday’s summit also agreed measures linking the two sides’ emissions-trading schemes and allowing young people to study and work across U.K.-EU borders.

    On Thursday, Burnham’s government formally introduced into Parliament the legislation required to implement the trade and electricity agreements.

    Recent findings suggest that lawmakers will get their first chance to debate them on Dec. 7, with a vote expected to follow, Labour confirmed Thursday.

    The EU Partnership Bill, which the government also refers to as the “Cutting Costs” bill, will almost certainly be approved by the lower House of Commons, where Labour holds a large majority.

    In a recent development, it will see the U.K. align with EU rules for sectors covered by the agreements, something known as dynamic alignment.

    Sources indicate that the U.K. government claims linking the pair’s carbon markets would create the world’s largest connected carbon market and exempt 6.5 billion pounds’ ($8.1 billion) worth of British exports from EU carbon border taxes.

    London and Brussels have given themselves six more months to reach agreement on reduced university tuition fees for EU students in Britain, a key demand of the bloc.

    Having previously remarked he would like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, Burnham has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.

    Industry observers note that the prime minister has vowed to present his options to the public after a year of “informal brainstorming” with the EU. He stated this week that rejoining without a referendum would be “unthinkable.”.

    Several former Conservative prime ministers, including Rishi Sunak, Boris Johnson, Theresa May and David Cameron, have warned against reopening a debate that deeply divided the country.

    Reform leader Nigel Farage remarked this week he would “repeal” the reset deal while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Thursday she “does not support” what Burnham is doing.

    By PETER HUTCHISON Agence France-Presse.

    #216020. Heading into the Thanksgiving break

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2171 w)
