    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Heading into the Thanksgiving break

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers!
    • Following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30.
    • On Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers! We are very grateful for your support of our work. If you’d like to learn more about what the Supreme Court has stated about Thanksgiving, you can revisit our Closer Look on the topic from this time last year.

    Following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30. The justices will hear eight total oral arguments during this session, addressing such issues as the Second Amendment, deportations to “third-party countries,” and the seizure of an airplane over the illegal transportation of beer.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v. Cook County, on whether the Second Amendment guarantees a right to possess AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, but it did not take action on Cook County’s request to dismiss the case as moot. On Tuesday, the court announced that it had deferred action on that request until after oral argument, which will take place on Wednesday, December 2. The case name is now Khaya v. Cook County. For more on Tuesday’s announcement, see the On Site section below.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed tomorrow and Friday for Thanksgiving.

    In a recent development, the December argument session will begin on Monday. That day, the justices will hear oral arguments in two cases: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, on whether Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding, allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination; and Wassily v. Blanche, on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Jouppi v. Alaska, an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane over the transport of beer into a dry village.

    On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Khaya v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, at 10:00 a.m. EST. As noted above, we will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Jack Birle, Washington Examiner.

    In June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled “in Carson v. Makin that Maine could not exclude religious schools from a state program that allows parents to use vouchers for public or private schools for their children.” Now, a group of Catholic schools has asked the justices to revisit the program and address rules that were passed while the earlier case was pending “to bar schools from participating ... if their admissions policies prefer students of a certain religion, allow religious discrimination in their schools, or do not follow the state’s views on gender ideology,” according to the Washington Examiner. “The Catholic schools urge the Supreme Court to address multiple questions if it takes up the case, including whether to overrule the 1990 Supreme Court ruling Employment Division v. Smith, which found that the free exercise clause does not allow for people to violate a law as part of their religious practice, as long as the law is valid and neutral in how it is applied. The petition ... argues that Smith has allowed Maine to continue to exclude religious schools from state programs.”.

    Attorneys for Emily Bickford, a Maine mother “who has been prohibited from taking her 13-year-old daughter to church” in a custody order, appealed her challenge to the order to the Supreme Court last week. The order allows the child’s father “to solely decide on his daughter’s involvement with Calvary Chapel Church.” Bickford asks the justices to find that it violates “parental rights and religious liberty protections,” according to WMTW in Portland, Maine. “A parent’s ability to take her child to church during her own parenting time now depends on the State in which she lives,” Bickford’s petition for review says. “When a state court strips a fit parent of her right to direct her child’s religious upbringing and vests a co-parent with veto power, it deploys the coercive authority of the State to extinguish a fundamental right.”.

    Kanishka Singh and Julia Harte, Reuters.

    On Tuesday, “Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a symbol for critics of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, left the US for Spain,” according to Reuters. His voluntarily departure brought an end to “a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.” It began when “US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.” For months, officials “said they could not bring him back,” but the Supreme Court ultimately “ordered the government [to] facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return.” After he returned to the United States in June 2025, Abrego Garcia faced human smuggling charges “stemming from an earlier incident” and a renewed deportation effort.

    Gavin Bade, The Wall Street Journal.

    Since February, when the Supreme Court held that President Donald Trump did not have the authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs, the Trump administration has been using other statutes to rebuild the president’s tariff regime. This week, that effort will continue when the administration announces increased “tariffs on China and dozens of other countries,” according to The Wall Street Journal. “The upcoming tariffs will likely be added to levies from a separate tariff action, unveiled in July, that sought to penalize nations for not blocking the trade of goods produced with forced labor,” and target countries that the Trump administration has concluded are harming U.S. producers by “flood[ing] global markets with cheaper goods.” That July action sparked a new lawsuit over the administration’s tariff policies.

    On Monday, a panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with President Donald Trump “in his fight to overturn his hush money criminal conviction in New York, ruling that a judge wrongly denied his effort to move the case into federal court,” according to The Hill. Trump’s current push to transfer the case “cites the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling.” The president contends that “he has the legal right to bring it up before a federal judge as a defense,” and the 2nd Circuit panel held on Monday that the district court did not properly consider this argument. “Monday’s decision effectively puts a halt to Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s state court system and moves it to federal court, where the president will continue pressing his arguments that the case should remain there.”.

    Philip Jankowski, The Dallas Morning News.

    In a recent development, texas’ Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson mentioned he will not defend the state’s “Ten Commandments classroom law,” just weeks before the justices are expected to consider whether to take up a challenge to it, according to The Dallas Morning News. “My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional,” Johnson said. “The court will have the ultimate say as to what’s constitutional and what is not, but I’m the one who states what the state’s position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken.” Outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton “cited Johnson’s unwillingness to defend the law as a reason the justices should decline to hear” the challenge to it in the state’s brief in opposition, which was filed on November 10. “If the Supreme Court stays out of the fight, a federal appeals court ruling upholding the classroom displays in Texas would remain in place, preserving a legal victory for Paxton even after he leaves office in January.”.

    It has been revealed that with just over a week remaining before the justices will hear argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case.

    On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the Closer Look section of this newsletter to covering the plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases. In this article, Blake took a step back and reflected on what we have learned.

    In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman analyzed each justice’s voting pattern in interim docket cases involving federal executive action, highlighting “a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.”.

    Industry observers note that in his Court Beyond Borders column, Martin Flaherty focused on the Supreme Court’s grant of review in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. The case, according to Flaherty, will put “the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law” in the spotlight.

    In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1978’s Federal Communications Commission v. Pacifica Foundation, holding that the government may “constitutionally prohibit indecency even” when it falls “short of legal obscenity.” In a dissenting opinion, Justice William Brennan criticized the majority for “attempt[ing] to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people.”.

    (SCOTUSblog Plus) Since joining in 2022, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has forged a unique role on the Supreme Court. It often appears, as Amy noted in this analysis, that Jackson’s goal in dissenting opinions is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision of the law and speak to the public directly – regardless of whether anyone else on the court agrees.

    In his SCOTUSCrim column on Friday, Rory Little aimed “to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law” and explore “why that can be so interesting.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French critique Congress’ current governing processes with the help of Michael “Frags” Fragoso, a partner at Torridon Law, and Nicholas Bagley, a professor of law at the University of Michigan and author of the book Why We Can’t Have Nice Things: How Legal Reformers Accidentally Broke America.

    The Closer Look in Wednesday editions is typically an entry in our Ask Amy series, in which Amy Howe answers reader questions about the Supreme Court.

    It has been revealed that Q: At least for those of us of a certain age, the November 9 order list contained a familiar name in the “Attorney Discipline” section: Larry Klayman, perhaps best known as a frequent and fervent foe of the Clinton administration, had been “disbarred from the practice of law” in the Supreme Court. Which leads to the question: How, exactly, does someone get disbarred from the Supreme Court bar – especially if, like Klayman, they’ve never argued there?

    A: The answer (like so many others) can be found in the Supreme Court’s rules, starting with the rule that outlines how someone becomes eligible to join the Supreme Court bar, which is necessary not only to argue before the justices but also to sign filings there: lawyers must have been (among other things) “admitted to practice” in another jurisdiction for at least three years, and they cannot have been subject to any disciplinary proceedings during that time.

    Sources indicate that because becoming a member of the Supreme Court bar requires a clean disciplinary record, it follows that disciplinary problems can get a lawyer kicked out of the Supreme Court bar – even if the underlying conduct had nothing to do with the court itself. Specifically, the court’s rules provide for the suspension of any lawyer who “has been disbarred or suspended from practice in any court of record, or has engaged in conduct unbecoming a member of the Bar of this Court.” The suspended lawyer then has the chance to try to persuade the court “why disciplinary action should not be taken,” after which the court may take “any appropriate disciplinary action,” which can include disbarment.

    In Klayman’s case, he was apparently suspended by the bar associations in the District of Columbia and Florida for alleged ethical violations in connection with his efforts to represent rancher Cliven Bundy in a federal court in Nevada, leading to his disbarment from the Supreme Court earlier this month. Klayman told Law360 that he intends to seek reconsideration of the Supreme Court’s order.

    “It is like having a new in-law at Thanksgiving dinner. Uncle Fred will put on a clean shirt.”.

    — Chief Justice John Roberts’ thoughts when a latest member joins the Supreme Court.

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Director of Technology Partnerships to lead the teams responsible for growing Supabase through technology integrations and our marketplace ecosystem.

    Industry observers note that you’ll bring together two complementary motions: partnerships that embed Supabase into the products developers already use, and a marketplace that helps developers discover and connect complementary technologies to their Supabase projects. Your job is to turn both into durable sources of revenue, adoption, and customer value.

    Reporting to the Head of Partnerships, you’ll lead and develop the Integrations and Marketplace teams, set their commercial strategy, and work hands-on with our most important partners. A central part of the role is working closely with AI labs to build strategic relationships, develop integrations, and bring joint opportunities to market. You’ll partner closely with Product, Engineering, Sales, Marketing, and Finance to take integrations from idea to launch—and grow their impact long after launch.

    This role is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, where you’ll build relationships with leading AI, developer tools, and infrastructure companies. Supabase is remote-first, and you’ll work across a globally distributed team.

    Lead, coach, and develop the Integrations and Marketplace partnerships teams, including team leads and partner managers.

    Set a clear strategy for where Supabase invests across strategic technology partnerships, marketplace categories, and emerging ecosystem opportunities.

    Define team objectives, partner coverage, investment priorities, and operating cadence. Make thoughtful tradeoffs between high-touch strategic partnerships and scalable programs.

    Build a culture of ownership, commercial discipline, and strong cross-functional execution.

    Drive revenue from technology integrations through partner-driven customer acquisition, product consumption, expansion, retention, co-sell opportunities, and commercial arrangements.

    Own the commercial performance of the technology partnerships and marketplace portfolio, including forecasting and reporting on progress, risks, and return on investment.

    Build and deepen relationships with AI labs, working closely with their product, engineering, business development, and executive teams to identify and execute high-impact partnership opportunities.

    Develop executive relationships with strategic partners across developer tools, cloud, and adjacent infrastructure.

    Lead or support negotiations for complex partnerships, including integration, referral, revenue-sharing, and joint go-to-market agreements.

    Help partner managers build joint business plans that connect partner priorities to measurable outcomes for Supabase and its customers.

    Lead and develop the Marketplace team, setting its commercial and partner strategy and holding the team accountable for outcomes.

    Guide the team in identifying the capabilities developers need, recruiting the right partners, and helping those partners launch and grow.

    Set priorities and allocate resources across strategic, high-touch partners and scalable paths for emerging and self-serve partners.

    Ensure the team works effectively with Product and Engineering on integration quality, partner onboarding, discovery, activation, and the developer experience across product surfaces.

    Enable the team to work with Marketing and Sales to launch integrations, enable teams, and drive ongoing adoption—not just announcements.

    Establish clear measures for partner-sourced and influenced pipeline, integration adoption, revenue, consumption, retention, and marketplace performance.

    Work with Finance, Data, and Partner Operations to improve attribution, reporting, forecasting, and partner revenue processes.

    Represent the voice of partners and customers in product and go-to-market planning, while aligning stakeholders around shared priorities.

    Identify risks early, remove blockers, and communicate decisions and outcomes clearly to leadership.

    Have significant experience in technology partnerships, business development, or ecosystem leadership at a developer tools, cloud, infrastructure, or SaaS manufacturer.

    Have led and developed partner-facing teams, including managers or senior individual contributors, and can balance strategic direction with hands-on execution.

    Have a track record of building partnerships that produced measurable revenue, product adoption, or customer growth.

    Have negotiated complex commercial agreements and understand partnership economics, including revenue share, referrals, and consumption-based models.

    Industry observers note that have worked closely with Product and Engineering to ship and grow technical integrations. You can engage credibly with technical teams, including those at AI labs, even if you aren’t the person writing the code.

    Know how to build relationships with executives while earning the trust of product, engineering, and go-to-market teams.

    Use data to prioritize opportunities, assess partner performance, and make decisions when attribution is imperfect.

    Are comfortable building in an evolving environment, communicating in writing, and working asynchronously across time zones.

    Built or scaled a developer marketplace, integration ecosystem, or partner platform.

    Worked with AI LLMs, AI app builders, databases, open-source products, or developer infrastructure.

    A background in software development, with an understanding of how developers build and integrate products.

    Experience growing both a small number of strategic partnerships and a broader, scalable partner program.

    A strong network in the San Francisco Bay Area technology ecosystem.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    It has been revealed that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    It has been revealed that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #216017. Judge doesn’t like your objections? Here are some tips to keep them coming in a meaningful way

    📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1079 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Judge doesn’t like your objections? Here are some tips to keep them coming in a meaningful way

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.
    • Industry observers note that sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction.
    • Porto, who specializes in appellate civil issues, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Juli M. Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.

    Industry observers note that sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction. Sometimes it’s a devastating ruling on key evidence. Sometimes the concern is the judge’s failure to stop opposing counsel from badgering a witness.

    Porto, who specializes in appellate civil issues, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.

    A principal at Blankingship & Keith in Fairfax, Virginia, Porto warns that typically, no matter how “egregious a trial judge’s error was, if it’s not preserved, it can’t be appealed.”.

    Sources indicate that litigators know they need to preserve the record during court hearings, depositions or trial. And they’re aware that they generally can’t raise an objection for the first time on appeal.

    But still, even the most experienced lawyers hesitate on how much to object and how far to go when advocating for their clients, particularly when judges appear to lose their patience.

    “It can be a delicate balance,” says J.C. Lore III, director of trial advocacy at Rutgers Law School. “Lawyers don’t want to make the judge angry.”.

    Rule 103 of the Federal Rules of Evidence advises lawyers that objections must be timely and done with specificity.

    While state rules of evidence vary, they tend to follow the same framework as the Uniform Rules of Evidence.

    In addition, the American Bar Association Model Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 requires lawyers to act competently.

    Tiffany Williams Brewer is chair of the ABA Section of Litigation and a former Fresh Jersey state administrative law judge. She notes a lawyer’s role is to “courteously remind” the judge of the importance of preserving the record.

    “As a former judge, I can relate that judges are often focused on the efficiency of moving the trial forward and may not even realize that they have skipped the opportunity to allow the lawyers to properly put their evidentiary basis on the record,” Brewer states.

    Most litigators have a war story or two where they felt they were being reasonable and advocating for their client while the judge was being unreasonable and obstructing them. And then there are the extreme cases.

    In a Bexar County, Texas, court in 2024, then-Judge Rosie Speedlin Gonzalez accused an attorney of coaching her client and then pushed back when the attorney objected.

    Gonzalez said the attorney was “not allowed to be argumentative and argue just for the sake of argument.”.

    As the situation escalated, she ordered the attorney to be handcuffed and placed in the jury box.

    In a recent development, gonzalez was later charged over the incident, then the charges were dropped when she agreed to resign and never again seek reelection. She declined comment to the ABA Journal.

    For the most part, Lore notes, judges know lawyers must make objections and don’t take it personally.

    However, Lore says, when lawyers are using objections as a tactic to disrupt or rattle opposing counsel, judges tend to get angry and push back.

    Amy M. Stewart is a partner at Fisher Phillips in Dallas and chair of the ABA Section of Litigation.

    “No one promised us in law school that making objections would be easy or without anxiety,” Stewart says.

    Sometimes, dealing with a judge who won’t let counsel make proper objections requires some strategic maneuvering, she adds.

    In one case, her firm hired an appellate lawyer to handle preserving the record during trial. Unfortunately, Stewart claims, the judge told the appellate lawyer to “sit down” at critical moments in the trial.

    “Appellate counsel held her own, but the drama was becoming distracting for the jurors,” Stewart states, so the trial team changed course, and had a male counsel make the objections.

    “We realized the court never interrupted one of our co-lead counsels on the case,” Stewart notes. “We coached him to make these critical objections, and the court would rule.”.

    During his decades of litigation, Jules Epstein has seen all kinds of issues come up during trial with judges who are reasonable and those who are less so. He suggests that if a judge is repeatedly blocking an attorney from making objections, the attorney should approach the judge calmly when the jury is not around.

    Industry observers note that “You can say to the judge, ‘I don’t want to violate your protocols, but I have to protect my client. Will you please give me instructions on how you want me to do this?’” claims Epstein, director of advocacy programs at Temple University Beasley School of Law.

    If that doesn’t work, he states, a lawyer can file a written pleading or motion to preserve objections, including every single effort made to object in a timely way.

    There’s also the option for an interlocutory appeal, depending on state rules, before a trial has concluded.

    There are times, indicates Ryan Watstein, that lawyers need to stand up to judges on behalf of their clients, even if that means they “catch a few black eyes” in the process.

    “There are a lot of things culturally built into the practice of law, including a tendency to be intentionally hesitant to push back, particularly on the judiciary,” says Watstein, an Atlanta-based litigator and founding partner of Watstein Terepka.

    In a LinkedIn post in May, Watstein described how he was trying to convince a judge to rein in opposing counsel during discovery. Watstein kept arguing, and the judge yelled, “This is your last chance, Mr. Watstein.”.

    Watstein explains that the courtroom was tense, and his client was uncomfortable. He thought he might get held in contempt.

    Sources indicate that “Every instinct our conservative profession teaches you was telling me to sit down,” Watstein claims. “But I didn’t sit down.”.

    Watstein says he kept talking, despite the judge indicating it was time to stop. He said that he would seek appellate review of the judge’s decision if he didn’t get justice on the problem.

    He ended up convincing the judge to reverse himself.

    Watstein warns against being “overly deferential” when an “injustice is being perpetrated” against your client.

    According to recent reports, “You should always start in way that is respectful and professional, but there are circumstances where you have to push harder,” Watstein says. “The line that lawyers are trained to go up to is not necessarily the appropriate stopping point.”.

    • Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers say the global water cycle has entered an âepoch of profound disruption.â.
    • (CN) â Global river flows and the amount of water held in lakes and reservoirs declined sharply during two years of exceptional heat, with freshwater resources falling to unprecedented levels in 2023 and 2024, researchers say in a new study published Thursday in Science.
    • River discharge worldwide dropped 5.7% during the period, while active water storage in lakes and reservoirs fell 9.5% compared with the 1991-2020 average.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers say the global water cycle has entered an âepoch of profound disruption.â.

    (CN) â Global river flows and the amount of water held in lakes and reservoirs declined sharply during two years of exceptional heat, with freshwater resources falling to unprecedented levels in 2023 and 2024, researchers say in a new study published Thursday in Science.

    River discharge worldwide dropped 5.7% during the period, while active water storage in lakes and reservoirs fell 9.5% compared with the 1991-2020 average. The losses were particularly severe in South America, where river flows fell nearly 18%, even as some areas experienced heavy rainfall and flooding.

    Led by Yongqiang Zhang, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences examined global freshwater trends from 1991 through 2025, combining measurements from 150 major river basins with satellite observations of more than 1.2 million waterbodies.

    Sources indicate that their analysis found that river flows and surface water storage fluctuated considerably between 1991 and 2006 before remaining relatively stable through 2022. Both measures then declined sharply in 2023 and 2024. River flows showed signs of rebounding in 2025, but the researchers stated the decline during the preceding two years was unprecedented in the historical record they examined.

    It has been revealed that south America was particularly hard hit. Streamflow fell 17.8%, while water held in lakes and reservoirs decreased 16.5%.

    âThe global water cycle has already entered an Anthropocene epoch of profound disruption,â the researchers write.

    The researchers linked the losses to the combined effects of two ocean climate patterns. El NiÃ±o, which develops in the Pacific Ocean, generally reduces rainfall across the Amazon. During the same period, unusually warm conditions in the tropical North Atlantic further disrupted the movement of moisture toward northern South America.

    That combination intensified the region’s water shortages, even as other areas received enough rain to produce flooding.

    Industry observers note that the findings show extreme heat can coincide with declining freshwater resources even in regions that typically receive abundant rainfall. Scientists have generally expected climate change to bring heavier precipitation to wet areas and increased evaporation in dry ones, but declining river flows and depleted soil moisture point to more complicated changes.

    Justices to consider whether noncitizens who lose asylum status may still obtain green cards

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v.
    • It has been revealed that although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v.
    • The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v. Blanche, a case on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    It has been revealed that although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on the Trump administration’s suspension of access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border – it may hold considerable consequences for noncitizens and bring new significance to the Trump administration’s effort to scale back asylum.

    The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.

    Tamer Wassily was granted asylum in 2000 after raising concerns about facing religious persecution in his home country of Egypt. The Department of Homeland Security moved to terminate Wassily’s asylum protections after he was convicted in 2004 of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, beginning the process of deporting him back to Egypt.

    In a recent development, byron Velasquez Arreaga came to the United States from Guatemala in 1995 and was granted asylum the following year. After Velasquez Arreaga was convicted of driving while intoxicated in 2015 and for aggravated driving while intoxicated in 2018, DHS indicated that it would terminate his asylum protections and move to deport him.

    Industry observers note that amid their removal proceedings, and after their asylum protections had been terminated, both Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga applied to become lawful permanent residents. This option is available to asylum recipients who meet certain requirements, including remaining in the United States for at least a year after receiving asylum protections, under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).

    After many years of complicated legal wrangling before immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals, the men’s cases were considered together by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. The question before that court – and the question that is now before the Supreme Court – was whether noncitizens like Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga remain eligible for adjustment of immigration status under Section 1159(b) after their asylum protections have been terminated, because the statute refers to “any alien granted asylum” but is silent as to whether applicants must currently be asylees.

    In a 2-1 ruling, a 2nd Circuit panel rejected the men’s contention that “granted asylum” addresses a past decision – in which case anyone who had ever received asylum would be eligible for status adjustment under Section 11159(b) – and concluded that noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated are “categorically barr[ed]” from applying for adjustment to permanent legal status.

    Sources indicate that writing for the majority, Judge Richard Wesley emphasized the use of the word “status” in the opening of Section 1159(b), which reads: “The Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General ... may adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum.” According to Wesley, a “natural reading of ‘the status of any alien granted asylum’ is that a noncitizen must presently be granted asylum to adjust to lawful permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).”.

    In a recent development, in January, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga asked the Supreme Court to review the 2nd Circuit’s ruling, highlighting a disagreement between the federal courts of appeals over whether the phrase “granted asylum” in Section 1159(b) “refer[s] to a completed, historical event” or “a continuing, present status.” Like the 2nd Circuit, they noted, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has held that noncitizens who have lost their asylum protections “are categorically ineligible” “for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status under Section 1159(b).” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, on the other hand, has held that such immigrants remain “eligible for adjustment.”.

    In late June, the justices granted review.

    Recent findings suggest that in their brief on the merits, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga contend that the 2nd Circuit’s decision is out of step with the “[t]ext, context, structure, history, and purpose” of Section 1159(b). In particular, they highlight several nearby passages in which lawmakers explicitly imposed “continuing conditions” that address a termination of immigration status, asserting that Congress “could have and would have” included such a condition here if it intended to unambiguously bar former asylees from applying for lawful permanent residency.

    Sources indicate that the two men also point to Section 1159(c), which grants the DHS secretary and attorney general the authority to waive portions of the statute “for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest.” Holding that adjustment to lawful permanent residency is categorically unavailable to noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated “would take core parts of that discretion away,” the men write. Such a limitation cuts against Congress’ purpose for allowing for discretion, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue. “There are many reasons why Congress would want” these officials “to retain discretion” here, they say, including that termination sometimes stems from factors “entirely outside” an asylee’s control. For example, the immigration status of the spouse and children of an asylee is often linked to the asylee’s status. If the noncitizen who was originally granted asylum loses his or her status, so does the whole family.

    Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga ask the justices to recognize that, at the very least, the text of Section 1159(b) is unclear and to apply the rule of lenity, which they describe as a “well-settled and longstanding principle” under which “ambiguous provisions leading to the severe sanction of removal should be construed in favor of the noncitizen.” The Supreme Court “has repeatedly restated and reaffirmed that rule,” they conclude.

    Industry observers note that in its merits brief, the federal government counters that Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s interpretation of Section 1159(b) defies common sense. The text of the statute, according to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, describes a “transition from one status (that of an ‘alien granted asylum’) to another (that of an ‘alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence’).” If an immigrant is no longer at that starting point because his asylum status has been terminated, he can’t make the transition, Sauer asserts.

    Industry observers note that the government contends that the “statutory context” supports this interpretation, because, in nearby passages, “alien granted asylum” clearly refers to a noncitizen’s “present status.” For example, in Section 1158(c)(1), “Congress identified benefits available to an ‘alien granted asylum,’ including protection from removal and work authorization,” according to Sauer. “Those benefits undisputedly cease when asylum status is terminated.”.

    In a recent development, the government rejects the idea that barring noncitizens who have lost their asylum status from applying for a green card would interfere with the authority of the DHS secretary and attorney general to exercise discretion. Officials, Sauer writes, would remain free to intervene at an earlier point to prevent the termination of asylum status in the first place.

    Industry observers note that sauer concludes by urging the justices to reject what he characterizes as a “last-resort appeal to lenity” – that is, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s claim that Section 1159(b) is an “ambiguous provision[]” and should therefore be interpreted in their favor. He argues that the rule of lenity does not apply here, not just because the meaning of the provision is clear, but also because Section 1159(b) does not directly address deportation, which is the context in which the rule of lenity arises.

    The Supreme Court’s decision in Wassily v. Blanche is expected by early July at the latest.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #216006. Industry News: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1876 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding.
    • In a recent development, the plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system.
    • Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at concern clearly authorizes them.

    In a recent development, the plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit considered Crowther’s and Joseph’s cases together. It held that Title IX does not provide a right – either explicitly or by implication – for employees to sue for sex discrimination. When the full court declined to reconsider their case, Crowther and Joseph asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which it agreed in May to do.

    Sources indicate that crowther and Joseph urge the justices to reverse the 11th Circuit’s decision and allow their lawsuits to go forward. They point to the text of Title IX, which provides that “[n]o person … shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” That language, they say, creates a broad ban on sex discrimination by schools that receive federal funding; moreover, they add, Title IX “also contains ‘a list of narrow exceptions’ that does not include employment discrimination” – further evidence that Congress intended Title IX’s ban on sex discrimination to apply to both employees and students.

    Sources indicate that the Georgia university system agrees that Title IX bars sex discrimination in employment, “and that federal agencies may deny funding to violators.” But that is not the question before the court, it stresses. Instead, it emphasizes, the glitch is whether Title IX allows employees to bring private lawsuits alleging that they were the victims of sex-based discrimination. The answer, the university system indicates, is no.

    To support their position, Crowther and Joseph cite several past Supreme Court rulings, including its 1982 decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell. In Bell, the court upheld regulations, meant to implement Title IX, that barred sex-based discrimination against employees (as well as students) at federally funded educational institutions. That decision, they say, demonstrates that Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination in employment. “The Court’s cases, read together,” they continue, “lead to the inexorable conclusion that an employee who is a victim of intentional sex-based discrimination by a federally funded education program or activity has a private right of action to seek damages under Title IX.”.

    It has been revealed that crowther and Joseph add that the Supreme Court has allowed employment discrimination lawsuits under other federal antidiscrimination statutes that apply to the recipients of federal funds – Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which prohibits discrimination based on disability. Those laws, they write, contain “virtually identical” language – further evidence that Title IX allows lawsuits like theirs.

    Sources indicate that the university pushes back against the employees’ attempt to draw comparisons with other federal antidiscrimination laws. It writes that Supreme Court “has assumed,” but has never specifically held, that “Title VI permits private suits for the narrow category of employment discrimination that statute prohibits.” But in any event, it notes, that assumption does not indicate anything about whether Congress created a private remedy in Title IX. The university system also emphasizes that “[t]he Rehabilitation Act has always been a far more detailed and targeted statute than Title IX” – for example, it “expressly ban[s] disability discrimination by the federal government as [an] employer.”.

    Sources indicate that similarly, the university system continues, the Supreme Court’s decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell does not resolve the question before the justices now. The court in that case, it writes, “had no reason to, and did not, consider whether Congress created a private remedy atop the express one the challenged regulations implemented.”.

    Whether the availability of another remedy forecloses private lawsuits under Title IX.

    Sources indicate that the Supreme Court, the university system writes, has made clear that the right to bring a private lawsuit hinges on whether there is “evidence confirming that Congress sought to” provide such a right. And when Congress has created “an express remedy” in another statute, there is “a strong ‘presumption’ that Congress did not imply others” – particularly when that “express remedy” involves a “‘comprehensive’ remedial scheme.”.

    That is exactly what happened here, the university system argues. “Mere weeks before Congress passed Title IX,” the university contends, “it extended … [the] protection—and reticulated enforcement scheme” in Title VII to school employees, which bars employment discrimination based on (among other things) sex. Therefore, the university system indicates, allowing lawsuits like Crowther’s and Joseph’s to go forward under Title IX “would attribute to the same Congress an inexplicable about-face: Immediately after giving a set of employees a private employment-discrimination remedy mediated by a ‘detailed administrative and judicial process,’ it silently gave the same employees a second private right of action, to attack the same basic harm.” And it did so, the university system suggests, without requiring employees to comply with any of the “strings attached” to private lawsuits under Title VII – including, but not limited to, the requirement to first file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission before going to court and its limits on the damages that can be recovered.

    Crowther and Joseph counter that “Title IX and Title VII are ‘vastly different.’” The prospect “that an employee might be able to bring a claim under both Title IX and Title VII does not justify” a determination that a private right of action is not available under Title IX. Rather, they write, the Supreme Court “has recognized that Congress has enacted overlapping remedies to eradicate employment discrimination, and Congress chose not to exclude employment discrimination from Title IX’s broad reach.”.

    Sources indicate that as additional support for the idea that Title IX does not provide a private right of action for employees, the university system notes that the law was enacted pursuant to Congress’ power under the Constitution’s Spending Clause, which gives Congress the power to impose taxes and spend money for (among other things) the country’s “general welfare.” In exchange for the federal funds, the recipients therefore agree to comply with the conditions that Congress imposes, and Congress can terminate the funding if a recipient fails to do so. However, in cases such as last term’s Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety, the Supreme Court has held that additional sanctions for violating the conditions in a law, such as the ability to bring a private lawsuit, are only available if the recipient has knowingly and voluntarily agreed to those sanctions. Here, the university system asserts, “Title IX does not unambiguously authorize private employment-discrimination suits,” and so it could not have known that it could be sued by employees, much less have agreed to that possibility.

    Crowther and Joseph reject this argument. They say that recipients of Title IX funds “‘have been on notice that they could be subjected to private suits for intentional sex discrimination under Title IX since 1979.’” As a result, they write, the Supreme Court’s “Spending Clause precedents ‘do[] not preclude private suits for intentional acts that clearly violate Title IX.’”.

    Industry observers note that A “friend of the court” brief from West Virginia and 20 other states attempts to refute this assertion. The states tell the justices that the states “are best positioned to say what Title IX’s bargain contains, as they’re the ones who’ve accepted it.” And they “can say with firsthand authority that the deal they made did not include this,” they write. “To the contrary, all the circumstances suggested to the States that Title VII [procedures, not private lawsuits] was the rightful home for those cases.”.

    It has been revealed that the Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting the university system, urges the justices not to reach the Spending Clause question at all. Instead, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the justices, they “should decide this case on the ground that” the employees’ “claims fail as a matter of ‘statutory interpretation’ alone.” Therefore, he writes, it is “unnecessary to reach, and prudent to avoid, the parties’ further dispute over the constitutional notice requirement for legislation enacted under Congress’s spending power.”.

    The possible effects of the court’s decision.

    Both the Trump administration and lawyers representing public school districts warn that a ruling in the employees’ favor could have “significant adverse consequences.” The federal government suggests that allowing lawsuits like the employees’ to go forward “would crowd judicial dockets with premature lawsuits that could often be avoided through proper use of Title VII’s administrative process, which successfully resolves numerous cases. And it would undermine the government’s primary authority to enforce both Title VII … and Title IX.”.

    In a recent development, for its part, the National School Attorneys Association emphasizes that “public school districts typically operate with limited legal and administrative staff. Expanding Title IX’s implied private right of action to cover claims against employees,” it says, “would impose disproportionate compliance and litigation burdens on public school districts and diminish the limited resources they have to educate students.”.

    Industry observers note that but a brief from the National Education Association, supporting the employees, takes a contrary stance. It tells the justices that upholding the 11th Circuit’s decision “would remove a critical deterrent against sex-based mistreatment of educators, exacerbate an already dire workforce crisis, and ultimately compromise the quality of education available to millions of students nationwide.” Lawsuits under Title VII, it writes, are not enough because that law “does not offer the full protections to which employees of education programs are entitled.”.

    A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    According to recent reports, recommended Citation: Amy Howe, Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX , SCOTUSblog (Nov. 25, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/court-to-hear-argument-on-whether-school-employees-may-bring-suit-under-title-ix/.

    Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • But wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime?
    • People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    But wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help users pass the time.

    AppLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    Sources indicate that gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    Now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s upcoming Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Sources indicate that some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    But, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    In a recent development, the Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    Bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    It has been revealed that to be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    But Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    In a recent development, but there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-upcoming businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    Apple is developing its own autonomous AI agents. [Bloomberg].

    Will Anthropic eventually launch an ads business? [Digiday].

    The Nasdaq enters its third correction of 2026 amid a painful tech investor slide. [NYT].

    #215998. The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1053 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
    • No tech giant has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
    • Sources indicate that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the tech giant selling the media sitting in the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

    No tech giant has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

    Sources indicate that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the tech giant selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

    Industry observers note that so what changed? TTD latched onto a latest principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the firm built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

    It has been revealed that as DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

    If The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a new era for the organization:.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The company should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

    Industry observers note that 2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

    Recent findings suggest that 3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

    From the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data remarked it would work for the buyer.

    TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the organization’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

    The business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

    Sources indicate that in 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

    In a recent development, redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

    Recent findings suggest that advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

    The concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

    In a recent development, television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

    Advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

    None of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

    CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only organization in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

    Industry observers note that most turnarounds require a company to find a new reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

    When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

    #215995. Industry News: AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (696 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Stravito was rolled out roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.
    • Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution.
    • At the crux of the tech giant is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Stravito was rolled out roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.

    Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution. Stravito, which touts itself as a consumer intelligence platform, uses AI to help marketers better understand their customers’ preferences and predict their reactions to ads.

    At the crux of the tech giant is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.

    Indeed, it’s the crux of the firm name: Stravito is a portmanteau of the words “strategy” and “vito,” which comes from the Latin word for life, “vita.”.

    In September, it launched its AI Persona Builder product, which uses brands’ data to develop AI personas that reflect their audiences.

    It has been revealed that stravito connects to a brand’s first-party data as well as other sources, like surveys and syndicated research, plus Stravito’s data from prior campaigns. From there, it builds out different AI personas for different audiences. The personas can represent smaller, more niche audiences, like people from a specific geo to capture “regional nuances,” stated Philogène, or broader audiences, like millennials or Gen Z. Marketers can ask a persona a specific question, like why they prefer one version of an ad over another, “and get instant feedback,” he added.

    Coffee brand Lavazza, for instance, conducted several thousand consumer interviews that it was able to integrate into the personas it built with Stravito. When Lavazza was testing different styles of packaging for its Dolcevita line of coffee, it was able to get feedback on the different variations from a relevant customer persona.

    Sources indicate that for this particular launch, Lavazza tested its US audience persona, which was built on data, including roughly 5,000 consumer interviews conducted through Kantar and research by the National Coffee Association. The research “covered consumers’ broader attitudes toward life, not only their attitudes toward coffee,” remarked Philogène, which helped with aesthetic decisions.

    Based on the persona’s responses to the colors and other visual cues, Lavazza ultimately changed the packaging color from black to dark blue, Philogène said. It then validated the decision by testing the newly introduced designs on Meta and comparing engagement.

    In a recent development, but rather than just spitting out recommendations and hoping that marketers will trust the personas’ responses at face value, Stravito takes a “glass box” approach to AI, said Philogène. This means that every suggestion and piece of feedback that the AI generates is accompanied by the specific sources and citations that informed it.

    Sources indicate that when your boss asks why you’re making a certain investment, “you do not want to tell them, you know, because AI told me so,” quipped Philogène. Instead, Stravito backs up its decision with the data sources it’s connected to.

    Industry observers note that but no matter how much research a brand or tech vendor has access to, no AI tool can accurately answer every question that someone may pose. And Stravito is exceedingly aware of that. Before a user even asks a question, remarked Philogène, the AI persona will note topics that it doesn’t have enough data to answer questions about, such as a brand’s pricing model.

    Recent findings suggest that an AI tool’s lack of knowledge can be “a feature, not a bug,” said Philogène. It’s crucial for brands to understand what data they’re lacking and where they should commission extra data, he added.

    According to recent reports, stravito’s AI “won’t be sycophantic” and just tell users what they want to hear, said Philogène. (Take that, ChatGPT.) Rather, it first determines whether or not it has enough data to answer a given question, and if it does, it specifies whether the answer is explicitly stated in the original source versus inferred. That way, the user can understand the logic backing up every one of the model’s conclusions.

    Having the necessary sources to back up one’s claims and decisions is a crucial facet of journalism, law and research, Philogène said. Shouldn’t advertising be held to the same standard?

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

    So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

    The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.

    The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

    Industry observers note that other changes to the documentation are less notable, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”.

    Marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search owners. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

    Plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently introduced “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

    But AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

    Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

    On Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

    Recent findings suggest that all that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

    Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

    In a recent development, it’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for consumers.

    Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

    Only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research indicates that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

    Ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”.

    It has been revealed that while the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

    Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

    Would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media].

    Don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek].

    It has been revealed that microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age].

    Industry observers note that after Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the tech giant has appointed its fresh CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch].

    It has been revealed that agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post].

    CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog].
